alignment.note: The Vulgate transmits an entirely different pericope (Mark 9:38, John's report about the exorcist), whereas the Greek and Peshitta preserve Mark 9:37 (the saying about receiving a child). This represents a verse-level textual displacement in the Vulgate manuscript tradition used for the Clementine edition.

Greek uses the relative pronoun ὃς with the modal particle ἂν to form an indefinite relative clause ('whoever'); Peshitta employs ܟܠ ܡܢ ('all who'), a functionally equivalent Semitic construction using a universal quantifier plus relative particle.

Greek uses the cardinal numeral ἓν ('one') with partitive genitive τῶν τοιούτων παιδίων ('of such children'); Peshitta uses the comparative particle ܐܝܟ ('like') with demonstrative ܗܢܐ ('this') plus ܛܠܝܐ ('child'), yielding 'like this child' rather than 'one of such children'—a stylistic simplification avoiding the partitive construction.

Greek employs the preposition ἐπὶ with dative article τῷ ὀνόματί μου ('in/upon the name of me'), a Hellenistic idiom for agency or authority; Peshitta uses the simple prepositional phrase ܒܫܡܝ ('in my name'), omitting the article (Syriac lacks the definite article in this construction) but preserving semantic equivalence.

Greek uses the emphatic pronoun ἐμὲ as direct object with the verb δέχεται ('receives me'); Peshitta employs the prepositional phrase ܠܝ ('to me') with the third-person pronoun ܗܘ ('he') plus participle ܡܩܒܠ ('receiving'), forming a periphrastic construction—syntactically distinct but semantically identical.

Greek repeats the indefinite relative ὃς ἂν ('whoever'); Peshitta uses ܘܡܢ ܕ ('and who'), where the conjunction ܘ is fused with the relative particle ܡܢ ܕ—a standard Syriac idiom for continuing parallel clauses without repeating the universal quantifier ܟܠ.

Greek uses the simple negation οὐκ ἐμὲ δέχεται ('does not receive me'); Peshitta employs the negative particle ܠܐ with the verb ܗܘܐ ('is') plus ܠܝ ܡܩܒܠ ('receiving me'), forming a periphrastic negative construction typical of Syriac syntax—functionally equivalent but structurally more elaborate.

Greek uses the articular aorist participle τὸν ἀποστείλαντά με ('the one having sent me') as a substantival construction; Peshitta employs the prepositional phrase ܠܡܢ ܕܫܕܪܢܝ ('to the one who sent me'), using a relative clause instead of a participle—syntactically distinct but semantically identical, reflecting Syriac preference for finite verbal forms over Greek participial constructions.
